questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
questions.prompt: A lining has nuclei at different heights. What additional observation best distinguishes pseudostratified from stratified epithelium?

options.text: Trace whether every cell reaches the basement membrane.
options.explanation: In pseudostratified epithelium all cells reach the basement membrane, although some do not reach the lumen; true stratification includes cells above the basal layer.

options.text: Count all nuclei seen in the section, regardless of cell boundaries.
options.explanation: Nuclear height or the total number of nuclear profiles alone cannot establish the number of epithelial layers.

options.text: Check whether the superficial cells are taller than they are wide.
options.explanation: Surface-cell shape helps name an epithelium, but columnar cells can occur in both arrangements.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
questions.prompt: A model exchange surface changes from one thin cell layer to several layers. With other variables fixed, what is the most direct consequence?

options.text: Diffusion becomes faster because there are more cells.
options.explanation: Adding layers increases the diffusion path; cell number alone does not improve passive exchange.

options.text: The diffusion path increases, making passive exchange slower.
options.explanation: A thin barrier shortens the path for diffusion. Several layers may help resist abrasion but impose a longer exchange path.

options.text: Transport is unchanged as long as the surface area is unchanged.
options.explanation: Diffusion depends on barrier thickness as well as area and the concentration or partial-pressure gradient.

questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.title: Amino-acid nitrogen and urea
questions.prompt: Why can transferring an amino group to glutamate not, by itself, complete nitrogen disposal?

options.text: The nitrogen has changed carrier but still needs a route to elimination.
options.explanation: Transamination redistributes nitrogen. The amino nitrogen must still be processed and ultimately excreted; the carbon skeleton follows its own metabolic fate.

options.text: Transamination always converts the amino nitrogen directly into urea.
options.explanation: Urea formation requires the urea-cycle reactions. An amino-group transfer is not the complete disposal pathway.

options.text: Once nitrogen reaches glutamate it cannot enter another pathway.
options.explanation: Glutamate collects and transfers nitrogen; it is a metabolic intermediate rather than a permanent endpoint.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Predict a renal circuit response
questions.prompt: In the fixed-pressure two-resistor model, double efferent resistance while keeping afferent resistance at 1. What happens relative to baseline?

options.text: Flow falls and glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: Total resistance increases, lowering flow. A larger share of the fixed pressure drop is across the efferent resistance, raising pressure upstream of it. This circuit does not calculate GFR.

options.text: Flow and glomerular pressure both fall.
options.explanation: Flow falls, but efferent resistance is downstream of the glomerular node; pressure at that node rises in this fixed-pressure model.

options.text: Flow rises because glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: Pressure at an intermediate point is not the same as flow through the circuit. Total resistance has increased.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Predict a renal circuit response
questions.prompt: Now double only afferent resistance. Which prediction follows from the same model?

options.text: Flow falls but glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: That was the downstream-resistance manipulation. Increasing upstream resistance lowers pressure at the glomerular node.

options.text: Flow and glomerular pressure both fall.
options.explanation: The total resistance rises and more of the pressure drop occurs before the glomerular node. This is a circuit prediction, not a clinical GFR estimate.

options.text: Flow is unchanged because arterial pressure is fixed.
options.explanation: A fixed driving pressure does not fix flow when total resistance changes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Real section A
questions.prompt: Which classification best describes the lining of the large open tubule in section A?

options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium
options.explanation: The lining forms one layer of cells with roughly similar height and width. Follow a single tubule wall; nearby tubules are separate structures, not extra epithelial layers.

options.text: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
options.explanation: Several adjacent tubules can mimic layers. A stratified epithelium has multiple layers within one lining between its basal boundary and free surface.

options.text: Simple squamous epithelium
options.explanation: Squamous cells are flattened. These tubular cells have appreciable cytoplasm around rounded nuclear profiles.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Transfer section B
questions.prompt: How should the thick lining facing the broad pale space in section B be classified?

options.text: Simple columnar epithelium
options.explanation: One layer of tall cells would connect the basal boundary to the surface. This lining contains many cell layers.

options.text: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
options.explanation: Uneven nuclear heights alone do not make an epithelium stratified. Here the tissue has distinct stacked layers with flattening toward the free surface.

options.text: Stratified squamous epithelium
options.explanation: Multiple layers lie between the basal boundary and the free surface. Superficial cells flatten, so classification uses the surface cells rather than the deeper rounded cells.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
questions.prompt: In a simplified plexus map, trace a C5 fibre into the axillary nerve. Which route fits?

options.text: Upper trunk → posterior division → posterior cord
options.explanation: C5 contributes to the upper trunk; its posterior division contributes to the posterior cord, from which the axillary nerve arises.

options.text: Upper trunk → anterior division → lateral cord
options.explanation: The upper trunk is correct, but its anterior division contributes to the lateral cord, not the cord giving rise to the axillary nerve.

options.text: Lower trunk → posterior division → posterior cord
options.explanation: The cord fits, but the usual lower trunk combines C8–T1 rather than C5.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
questions.prompt: A model shows the three cords beside an artery deep to pectoralis minor. What identifies the landmark used to name the cords?

options.text: The axillary artery before it reaches pectoralis minor
options.explanation: That is the first part. Cord names refer to their relations to the second part.

options.text: The second part of the axillary artery
options.explanation: Pectoralis minor divides the artery into parts; the second part lies deep to the muscle and defines the cord names.

options.text: The brachial artery below teres major
options.explanation: This is distal to the axillary artery and is not the landmark defining the cord names.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A superficial injury removes an epithelial lining while deeper smooth muscle remains intact. Which immediate functional loss follows most directly from the tissue that was removed?

options.text: All active force generation in the deeper muscle is abolished
options.explanation: The scenario preserves the deeper muscle. Loss of epithelial cells does not by itself establish loss of all muscle contraction.

options.text: The continuous protective barrier is disrupted
options.explanation: Epithelial continuity and cell junctions help maintain a barrier. Removing the lining exposes underlying tissue even when deeper contractile cells remain.

options.text: The extracellular collagen necessarily disappears from the supporting tissue
options.explanation: Collagen belongs to the supporting matrix. Its disappearance is not implied by selective removal of the epithelial layer.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: An unknown pink bundle has sparse flattened nuclei between abundant parallel extracellular fibres. No striations are seen. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Dense regular connective tissue, because matrix dominates over cells
options.explanation: Abundant aligned extracellular collagen with relatively sparse flattened fibroblast nuclei supports dense regular connective tissue such as tendon. This uses positive architectural clues.

options.text: Smooth muscle, because absent striations identify a non-striated contractile bundle
options.explanation: Absent striations are not specific to smooth muscle. The positive findings here are abundant extracellular fibres and sparse flattened nuclei, which favour dense regular connective tissue.

options.text: Skeletal muscle cut obliquely, because orientation can conceal its striations
options.explanation: An oblique cut can obscure striations, but it does not explain a field dominated by extracellular collagen with sparse flattened nuclei. The stated architecture supports connective tissue.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Selective myelin injury affects a peripheral nerve while its axons initially remain intact. Which functional prediction and glial-cell attribution are best supported?

options.text: Conduction may slow or fail, and the affected myelin was formed by oligodendrocytes
options.explanation: The functional prediction is plausible, but the cell attribution is incorrect. Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin; the question specifies a peripheral nerve.

options.text: Conduction must remain normal because the axons are still present
options.explanation: Axonal continuity does not guarantee normal conduction. Damage to insulating myelin can impair action-potential propagation even while the axon is initially intact.

options.text: Conduction may slow or fail, and the affected myelin was formed by Schwann cells
options.explanation: PNS myelin comes from Schwann cells and supports efficient action-potential propagation. This predicts a functional disturbance without assuming the whole neuron has died.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical teaching image is a transverse section viewed from the feet towards the head, with anterior at the top. A marker is in the upper-left part of the display. Which description follows from this orientation?

options.text: Patient’s left and posterior
options.explanation: This reverses both supplied orientation cues. The patient’s left appears on the display’s right, and posterior is at the bottom.

options.text: Patient’s right and anterior
options.explanation: Under the stated viewing convention, display-left corresponds to the patient’s right. The top of this image is explicitly labelled anterior.

options.text: Patient’s right and superior within the section
options.explanation: The patient’s side is correct, but superior is perpendicular to a transverse section. The top of this display is anterior, not superior.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical report describes fluid between the right visceral and parietal pleura. Which interpretation is anatomically justified?

options.text: Fluid is inside the right main bronchus
options.explanation: A bronchial lumen is within an airway. The report specifies a space outside the lung surface between pleural layers.

options.text: Fluid is in the pericardial cavity
options.explanation: The pericardial cavity is between serous pericardial layers, not pleural layers. The report identifies different boundaries.

options.text: Fluid occupies the right pleural cavity
options.explanation: The two named pleural surfaces define this space. This locates the fluid without establishing its cause or prescribing treatment.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical superficial mark lies on the anterior right forearm, closer to the wrist than to the elbow. Which statement remains justified when the person turns the palm down?

options.text: The mark remains on the anatomical anterior surface of the right forearm
options.explanation: Rotating the limb changes its displayed orientation, not the established anatomical name of its surface or its side.

options.text: The mark becomes posterior because it now faces away from the viewer
options.explanation: The viewer’s changing position cannot rename anatomical surfaces. Use the reference position to describe the mark consistently.

options.text: The mark proves an underlying nerve injury
options.explanation: Surface location alone does not establish damage to a deep nerve. Depth, function and additional observations would be needed.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In a simplified stomach-wall model, the epithelial lining remains intact while smooth-muscle contraction is reduced. Which function is most directly affected by the specified change?

options.text: The ability of the lining to form an epithelial barrier must be completely lost
options.explanation: Reduced muscle contraction does not itself establish epithelial destruction. The stem explicitly preserves the lining.

options.text: Mechanical mixing of the luminal contents
options.explanation: Smooth-muscle contraction contributes to mixing and propulsion. This prediction follows from the affected tissue’s function without assuming that every tissue has failed.

options.text: Chemical secretion by the intact epithelial lining is the function most directly reduced.
options.explanation: The lining is stated to remain intact; reduced smooth-muscle contraction most directly affects mechanical mixing and propulsion, although tissue functions can interact.

questions.title: Physiology Foundations: Membrane Transport and Resting Potential
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: In a teaching model, the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is inhibited while Na⁺ leaks continue. After the Na⁺ gradient weakens, what happens to the energy available for Na⁺-coupled glucose uptake?

options.text: It increases because the cotransporter starts hydrolysing ATP.
options.explanation: The cotransporter does not become an ATPase when the separate pump is inhibited.

options.text: It is unchanged because a protein transporter needs no gradient.
options.explanation: Secondary active transport depends on the coupled electrochemical gradient, not simply the presence of a protein.

options.text: It decreases because the downhill Na⁺ movement supplies less energy.
options.explanation: Weakening the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient reduces the driving force available to support uphill glucose transport.

questions.title: Physiology Foundations: Membrane Transport and Resting Potential
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A model membrane is permeable only to K⁺. Intracellular K⁺ stays fixed while extracellular K⁺ increases but remains below the intracellular concentration. What happens to the K⁺ equilibrium potential?

options.text: It becomes more negative.
options.explanation: Raising outside K⁺ reduces the outward concentration gradient; less negative voltage is needed to oppose it.

options.text: It becomes less negative.
options.explanation: The outside-to-inside K⁺ concentration ratio increases, shifting the K⁺ equilibrium potential in the positive direction.

options.text: It is unchanged because K⁺ is not actively transported through the channel.
options.explanation: The equilibrium potential depends on the concentration ratio even though movement through the channel is passive.

questions.title: Biochemistry Foundations: Enzymes, Kinetics and Regulation
questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.prompt: Under ideal reversible competitive inhibition, the active enzyme amount and other conditions stay fixed. Which pattern is predicted?

options.text: Higher apparent Km with unchanged Vmax.
options.explanation: More substrate is needed for half the limiting rate, but sufficient substrate can still approach the same Vmax.

options.text: Lower Vmax with unchanged apparent Km in every case.
options.explanation: This is the ideal pure non-competitive pattern, not the competitive model specified in the question.

options.text: Lower apparent Km with higher Vmax.
options.explanation: Competition does not increase catalytic capacity or reduce the substrate requirement in this model.

questions.title: Biochemistry Foundations: Enzymes, Kinetics and Regulation
questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.prompt: A hypothetical Michaelis–Menten assay has Vmax = 60 µmol/min and Km = 3 mmol/L. At [S] = 3 mmol/L, what is the initial rate?

options.text: 60 µmol/min
options.explanation: Vmax is the limiting rate approached at high substrate, not the rate when [S] equals Km.

options.text: 30 mmol/L
options.explanation: The numerical half is correct, but this is a concentration unit rather than a rate.

options.text: 30 µmol/min
options.explanation: At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2 = 30 µmol/min; the answer must retain rate units.

questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.subject: genetics
questions.prompt: In an Aa × Aa autosomal recessive cross, assume AA and Aa are unaffected and aa is affected. Before knowing the phenotype, what is the probability of an Aa carrier child?

options.explanation: One of the four combinations is AA and one is aa, but two are heterozygous carriers.
Aa and aA are the two heterozygous outcomes among four equally likely combinations, giving 1/2.

options.text: Two thirds
options.explanation: Two thirds is the carrier probability conditional on an unaffected child in this model. That condition has not been supplied.

questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.subject: genetics
questions.prompt: Two cell types contain the same intact gene, but one has much less of its mRNA. Which conclusion is justified by these observations alone?

options.text: RNA abundance differs; the gene need not be absent from either cell.
options.explanation: Different transcription or RNA stability can change mRNA abundance even when the DNA sequence is present in both cells.

options.text: The cell with less mRNA must have lost the chromosome.
options.explanation: The question states that the same intact gene is present; mRNA abundance alone does not show chromosome loss.

options.text: Both cells must contain equal amounts of functional protein.
options.explanation: DNA presence does not fix RNA or protein abundance, and function also depends on later processing and regulation.

questions.title: Biophysics Foundations: Diffusion, Osmosis and Membranes
questions.subject: biophysics
questions.prompt: Two compartments have equal initial hydrostatic pressure. A membrane passes water but not the dissolved solute. The right side has more solute particles per litre. What is the initial net water movement?

options.text: From right to left
options.explanation: That direction would increase the initial osmotic imbalance under the stated equal-pressure conditions.

options.text: No net movement because solute cannot cross
options.explanation: Solute impermeability does not prevent water movement; the membrane is explicitly permeable to water.

options.text: From left to right
options.explanation: Water initially moves towards the more concentrated impermeant-solute compartment when initial hydrostatic pressures are equal.

questions.title: Biophysics Foundations: Diffusion, Osmosis and Membranes
questions.subject: biophysics
questions.prompt: A model cell and bath initially have equal total osmolarity. The bath solute can enter the cell. Is unchanged cell volume guaranteed over time?

options.text: Yes, equal osmolarity always means equal tonicity.
options.explanation: Equal total particle concentration does not account for solute permeability or redistribution over time.

options.text: No; solute permeability and redistribution must also be considered.
options.explanation: A permeating solute can alter the effective osmotic gradient, so equal initial osmolarity does not guarantee stable cell volume.

options.text: Yes, provided diffusion uses no ATP.
options.explanation: Whether ATP is used does not determine tonicity; passive solute entry can still alter water balance.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
questions.prompt: A neutral solute has a higher concentration outside a model cell. The membrane is impermeable to it. What changes immediately if the concentration difference is removed without adding a transport pathway?

options.text: A rapid inward flux begins because the solute no longer needs a carrier.
options.explanation: Removing the gradient cannot create a pathway through an impermeable barrier.

options.text: There is still no appreciable membrane flux; now there is also no concentration driving force.
options.explanation: The barrier lacks a pathway both before and after the change. Removing the gradient also removes the potential driving force for net passive movement.

options.text: The membrane starts hydrolysing ATP to restore the gradient.
options.explanation: No ATP-dependent transporter is specified; a concentration change does not make the lipid bilayer an ATPase.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
questions.prompt: In a model epithelial cell, an apical protein couples inward Na⁺ movement to uphill glucose entry. A separate basolateral pump hydrolyses ATP to maintain the Na⁺ gradient. How should the apical protein be classified?

options.text: An ion channel, because Na⁺ moves through it.
options.explanation: The specified protein couples two solutes, including uphill glucose movement; it is a cotransporter, not an uncoupled ion pore.

options.text: A primary active pump, because the pathway ultimately depends on ATP.
options.explanation: The separate basolateral pump uses ATP directly. Indirect ATP dependence does not mean the apical cotransporter hydrolyses ATP.

options.text: A secondary active cotransporter, because it uses downhill Na⁺ movement to drive glucose entry.
options.explanation: The cotransporter uses energy stored in the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient, which the ATP-dependent pump maintains.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
questions.prompt: An open channel conducts a positively charged ion. Its concentration difference favours entry, but membrane voltage favours exit. What information is needed to predict net flow?

options.text: The combined electrochemical gradient, including ion concentrations and membrane voltage.
options.explanation: Chemical and electrical forces can oppose each other; their combined effect determines passive net flow through an open selective channel.

options.text: Only the concentration difference, because channels ignore electrical forces.
options.explanation: An ion is charged, so membrane voltage contributes to its driving force.

options.text: Only whether the channel has an ATP-binding site.
options.explanation: The question specifies an open channel. ATP binding is not the information that resolves opposing chemical and electrical forces in this model.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Resting potential and the action potential
questions.prompt: A selective K⁺ conductance increases in a model cell at −70 mV. E_K remains −90 mV and other conditions initially stay fixed. Which initial change is expected?

options.text: Depolarisation towards +90 mV
options.explanation: The specified potassium equilibrium potential is −90 mV. Reversing its sign changes the problem and does not follow from opening channels.

options.text: Hyperpolarisation towards −90 mV
options.explanation: At −70 mV, potassium’s driving force favours outward positive current; more K⁺ conductance initially pulls voltage towards E_K.

options.text: A more negative E_K even though concentrations are fixed
options.explanation: Channel number changes conductance. With temperature and concentrations fixed, it does not change the Nernst equilibrium potential.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Resting potential and the action potential
questions.prompt: A passive membrane’s voltage change would eventually reach 10 mV after a maintained current step. Its time constant is 20 ms. How much of that change has developed after 20 ms?

options.text: About 6.3 mV
options.explanation: The step response reaches 1 − exp(−1), about 63%, after one time constant: 0.63 × 10 mV ≈ 6.3 mV.

options.text: About 3.7 mV
options.explanation: About 37% remains after one time constant of a decay. This question asks about the rising response to a maintained step.

options.text: The full 10 mV
options.explanation: One time constant does not complete the response; the ideal exponential approaches its final value asymptotically.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Resting potential and the action potential
questions.prompt: At steady state, an ideal uniform passive cable has ΔV(x) = 10 exp(−x/λ) mV. What is ΔV at x = λ?

options.text: About 6.3 mV
options.explanation: That fraction describes the rise towards a final value in one time constant, not spatial decay over one length constant.

options.text: Exactly 10 mV
options.explanation: That is the value at the input location x = 0. A passive cable attenuates the voltage change with distance.

options.text: About 3.7 mV
options.explanation: At x = λ, exp(−x/λ) = exp(−1) ≈ 0.37. The remaining change is approximately 3.7 mV.

questions.subject: biophysics
questions.title: Action potentials and impulse propagation
questions.prompt: A second normal neuronal spike cannot be generated while many voltage-gated sodium channels remain inactivated. What best explains this absolute refractory interval?

options.text: Insufficient available channels for regenerative inward current
options.explanation: Inactivated sodium channels must recover before they can support another normal regenerative response in this simplified model.

options.text: The sodium–potassium pump must recreate the entire sodium gradient after each spike
options.explanation: A normal spike redistributes a small fraction of the bulk ions; immediate refractoriness mainly concerns channel state, not total gradient exhaustion.

options.text: The membrane has lost all permeability to potassium
options.explanation: Outward potassium current may still be present. Total loss of potassium permeability is neither required nor the stated cause.

questions.subject: biophysics
questions.title: Action potentials and impulse propagation
questions.prompt: A teaching diagram labels a spontaneous diastolic depolarisation followed by a mainly Ca²⁺-dependent upstroke. Which cell model best fits those stated features?

options.text: A typical myelinated neuronal axon
options.explanation: The standard axonal model has a fast sodium-dependent upstroke and does not require spontaneous diastolic depolarisation.

options.text: An ordinary ventricular working myocyte
options.explanation: Working ventricular cells have a fast sodium-dependent upstroke and a plateau; the stated pacemaker sequence is different.

options.text: A sinoatrial nodal pacemaker cell
options.explanation: The combination of spontaneous diastolic depolarisation and a calcium-dependent upstroke fits the nodal pacemaker model.

questions.subject: biophysics
questions.title: Action potentials and impulse propagation
questions.prompt: Two hypothetical axons have the same diameter and intact excitable membranes. One is normally myelinated and the other is not. Which mechanism supports faster conduction in the myelinated axon?

options.text: The same action potential travels through the myelin as an unchanged object
options.explanation: Propagation requires current spread and renewed membrane excitation, not movement of an intact spike through the insulating sheath.

options.text: Reduced internodal leakage and charging load, with regeneration at nodes
options.explanation: Myelin alters passive electrical properties between nodes, while voltage-gated currents regenerate the signal at nodes of Ranvier.

options.text: The sodium–potassium pump directly carries each spike to the next node
options.explanation: The pump maintains gradients over time. It is not the rapid local-current mechanism that propagates each spike.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
questions.prompt: In a controlled preparation, presynaptic excitation is intact but terminal calcium entry is prevented. Applied transmitter still evokes the usual postsynaptic response. Which stage is directly disrupted?

options.text: Postsynaptic receptor responsiveness
options.explanation: The direct-transmitter test shows that the postsynaptic apparatus can respond under the stated conditions.

options.text: Action-potential conduction to the terminal
options.explanation: The stem explicitly states that presynaptic excitation reaches the terminal; failure of arrival is not the specified defect.

options.text: Calcium-triggered transmitter release
options.explanation: Preventing calcium entry removes the normal rapid trigger for vesicle fusion while leaving the tested postsynaptic response possible.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
questions.prompt: Opening an inhibitory conductance whose reversal potential is near resting voltage produces little baseline voltage change but reduces a later excitatory voltage response. Which explanation fits?

options.text: Increased conductance lowers input resistance and shunts the excitatory input
options.explanation: With a reversal near rest, the added conductance can reduce the voltage change produced by excitatory current without a large baseline hyperpolarisation.

options.text: Any inhibitory input must first make the membrane much more negative
options.explanation: Inhibition can occur through shunting. A large hyperpolarisation is not required in the stated near-resting reversal-potential case.

options.text: The excitatory neurotransmitter has necessarily been enzymatically destroyed
options.explanation: The observation concerns postsynaptic electrical conductance. It does not establish a change in transmitter breakdown.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
questions.prompt: Assume a passive linear model at one recording site, a −70 mV baseline, a −55 mV firing threshold and two coincident +8 mV contributions. What does this simplified calculation predict?

options.text: A peak of −62 mV, still below threshold
options.explanation: That includes only one of the two stipulated simultaneous contributions. The model asks for their linear sum.

options.text: A peak of −54 mV, crossing the stated threshold
options.explanation: −70 + 8 + 8 = −54 mV, which is more positive than −55 mV. This is the peak predicted by the stipulated passive sum. In an excitable neuron, crossing threshold recruits regenerative currents; the calculation does not give the actual action-potential peak.

options.text: An action potential with exactly twice the usual amplitude
options.explanation: Adding graded inputs can reach threshold; it does not imply that the resulting regenerative action potential doubles in height.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
questions.prompt: At a healthy adult motor end plate, which comparison correctly separates the end-plate potential from the muscle action potential?

options.text: The end-plate potential is graded and local; the muscle action potential is regenerative and propagates
options.explanation: Ligand-gated cation conductance creates the local end-plate response, which can recruit voltage-gated sodium channels in adjacent muscle membrane.

options.text: Both are propagated action potentials generated by the same acetylcholine receptor channel
options.explanation: The acetylcholine receptor produces a local graded response. Propagation depends on a separate voltage-gated excitability mechanism.

options.text: The end-plate potential is generated inside the SR and then released into the cleft
options.explanation: The end plate is postsynaptic surface membrane. SR calcium release occurs later within the muscle excitation–contraction sequence.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
questions.prompt: A hypothetical adult skeletal fibre has normal T-tubule action potentials and normal SR calcium stores, but voltage-sensor coupling to RyR1 is selectively disrupted. What is most directly reduced?

options.text: Acetylcholine synthesis in the motor-neuron terminal
options.explanation: The stipulated defect is inside the muscle coupling machinery. It does not specify a transmitter-synthesis change upstream.

options.text: The amount of calcium stored in the SR before stimulation
options.explanation: The stem explicitly states that stores are normal before stimulation; reduced release is different from an initially empty store.

options.text: The stimulus-evoked cytosolic calcium rise and resulting force
options.explanation: Disrupted coupling prevents the normal signal from depolarisation to SR release, reducing troponin activation and force in the stated model.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
questions.prompt: Which ATP-dependent process contributes directly to normal skeletal-muscle relaxation?

options.text: ATP depletion locks myosin onto actin until calcium disappears
options.explanation: Loss of ATP impairs detachment and calcium reuptake. It is not the normal controlled mechanism of relaxation.

options.text: SERCA pumps cytosolic calcium back into the SR
options.explanation: ATP hydrolysis supports calcium reuptake, lowering cytosolic calcium and reducing activation of the thin-filament regulatory system.

options.text: ATP hydrolysis causes actin filaments to become shorter
options.explanation: Filaments slide rather than shorten during contraction, and normal relaxation does not depend on shrinking actin filaments.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Connective tissue and extracellular matrix
questions.prompt: A fictional longitudinal section shows parallel collagen bundles with slender flattened nuclei between them. No cells in lacunae are described. Which interpretation uses both positive clues?

options.text: Hyaline cartilage identified solely by abundant matrix
options.explanation: Abundant matrix alone is nonspecific. The parallel bundles and slender intervening nuclei support a fibrous connective-tissue pattern.

options.text: Dense regular connective tissue
options.explanation: The aligned collagen architecture and fibroblast-like nuclear pattern together support dense regular connective tissue; they do not alone identify a specific organ.

options.text: Bone identified solely by the presence of collagen
options.explanation: Bone contains collagen, but this description lacks positive bone architecture such as lamellae, osteocyte lacunae and canaliculi.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Connective tissue and extracellular matrix
questions.prompt: A paraffin section contains large clear cell profiles, thin cytoplasmic rims and flattened peripheral nuclei. What is the most defensible explanation?

options.text: White adipocyte morphology with lipid removed during processing
options.explanation: A large lipid droplet commonly displaces the nucleus. Routine processing can extract lipid, explaining the clear appearance without implying an empty living cell.

options.text: Brown adipose proven to be generating heat at the moment of sampling
options.explanation: Brown adipocytes generally have multiple droplets; a routine section does not directly measure thermogenesis.

options.text: Extracellular cartilage lacunae without surrounding cells
options.explanation: The described cellular outlines and peripheral nuclei fit adipocytes; cartilage requires a different cell–matrix relationship.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Connective tissue and extracellular matrix
questions.prompt: A bone specimen was decalcified before sectioning. What can a routine image of that section not directly establish?

options.text: Whether lamellar architecture is present
options.explanation: Decalcification can preserve interpretable organic matrix architecture, although preparation and sampling still affect the view.

options.text: Whether cell profiles occupy spaces in the matrix
options.explanation: Cell and lacunar relationships can remain visible after decalcification; those observations are distinct from measuring mineral.

options.text: The original mineral density of the living bone
options.explanation: The preparation removes mineral. Inferring its original quantitative density directly from that section would exceed the evidence.

questions.subject: genetics
questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.prompt: A hypothetical genomic report identifies a rare sequence variant but classifies its relationship to disease as uncertain. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: Rarity alone confirms that the variant caused the phenotype
options.explanation: Rarity is one kind of evidence, not proof of causation. The stated interpretation remains uncertain.

options.text: The uncertain classification proves that the variant is harmless
options.explanation: Uncertain significance does not establish either a pathogenic or a benign classification.

options.text: The variant is detected, but its causal significance remains unresolved
options.explanation: Detection and interpretation are separate. Additional evidence may change classification; the report does not establish a confirmed molecular diagnosis.

questions.subject: genetics
questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.prompt: A fictional laboratory assay is validated only to detect one specified familial single-nucleotide variant. Its result is negative. What does that result establish within the stated scope?

options.text: The assay did not detect that specified variant under its validated conditions
options.explanation: A targeted negative result answers the defined assay question. It does not exclude unrelated variants or all genetic causes.

options.text: No genetic variation exists anywhere in the person’s genome
options.explanation: The assay covers one defined variant, not the entire genome or every type of variation.

options.text: Every copy-number change and repeat expansion has been excluded
options.explanation: Those variant classes are outside the explicitly stated scope; their absence cannot be inferred from this test.

questions.subject: genetics
questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.prompt: Why is a reference genome useful when analysing a sequence difference?

options.text: It defines the only biologically normal sequence at every position
options.explanation: A reference is a comparison framework. A difference from it is not automatically abnormal or disease-causing.

options.text: It supplies a coordinate and comparison framework
options.explanation: A reference allows a difference to be described at a defined location. Clinical meaning still needs separate evidence.

options.text: It contains the complete genotype of every human population
options.explanation: A single reference does not represent all human variation; broader pangenome frameworks address some of these limitations.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Somatosensory pathways and thalamic integration
questions.prompt: A fictional lesion selectively interrupts the right dorsal column at the T10 cord segment. Considering the classic pathway from the feet, which signal is most directly interrupted before its crossing?

options.text: Right-foot vibration and conscious proprioception
options.explanation: Those first-order signals ascend in the right dorsal column to the medulla before the second-order pathway crosses.

options.text: Left-foot vibration because every sensory axon crosses at spinal entry
options.explanation: Dorsal-column body mechanosensory axons do not follow the spinal-entry crossing pattern of the main anterolateral pathway.

options.text: Right-face touch relayed through the spinal dorsal column
options.explanation: Much face sensation follows trigeminal pathways in the brainstem; it is not carried from the face through the thoracic dorsal column.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Somatosensory pathways and thalamic integration
questions.prompt: Which pairing describes the principal ventral posterior thalamic relays in this simplified somatosensory comparison?

options.text: VPL for face; VPM for body
options.explanation: That reverses the principal body-versus-face assignment used in this lesson.

options.text: The reticular nucleus for both direct third-order projections to S1
options.explanation: The reticular nucleus provides inhibitory modulation; it is not the principal ascending somatic relay projecting directly to S1.

options.text: VPL for body; VPM for face
options.explanation: Ventral posterolateral relays body information, while ventral posteromedial is associated with the main trigeminal face pathway.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Somatosensory pathways and thalamic integration
questions.prompt: A fictional lesion interrupts the right anterolateral tract at the T10 cord segment. Which principal signal from well below that level is most directly interrupted?

options.text: Right-foot vibration still ascending before its medullary crossing
options.explanation: This describes the right dorsal-column route, not the specified anterolateral tract.

options.text: Left-foot pain-temperature input that has already crossed in the spinal cord
options.explanation: The main left-sided pain-temperature pathway crosses near its entry levels and then ascends in the right anterolateral system.

options.text: Face touch that crossed at the T10 cord segment
options.explanation: The principal trigeminal face pathways relay and cross in the brainstem; T10 is not their crossing site.
